content: Type I hypersensitivity is mediated by the release of immunoglobulin E (IgE) from mast cells and basophils. This reaction is typically associated with allergic responses, such as anaphylaxis or hay fever. Type II hypersensitivity occurs when antibodies, specifically immunoglobulin G (IgG) and immunoglobulin M (IgM), bind to antigens present on the patient’s own cells. This binding marks the cells for destruction, leading to what is known as antibody-dependent or cytotoxic hypersensitivity. Examples include hemolytic anemia and certain drug reactions. Type III hypersensitivity is triggered by the deposition of immune complexes, which are aggregates of antigens, complement proteins, and IgG or IgM antibodies, in various tissues. These deposits can lead to inflammation and tissue damage, as seen in conditions like systemic lupus erythematosus and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Type IV hypersensitivity, also referred to as cell-mediated or delayed-type hypersensitivity, typically takes two to three days to develop. This reaction involves T cells, monocytes, and macrophages and is implicated in many autoimmune and infectious diseases. It can also manifest as contact dermatitis, such as the reaction to poison ivy. The adaptive immune system likely evolved with the first vertebrates, as invertebrates do not produce lymphocytes or antibody-based humoral responses. However, many invertebrates utilize mechanisms that appear to be precursors to vertebrate immunity. Even structurally simple organisms, such as bacteria, have immune-like systems, such as the restriction-modification system, which protects them from bacteriophages. Pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) are proteins used by nearly all organisms to identify pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs). Antimicrobial peptides, such as defensins, are evolutionarily conserved components of the innate immune response found in all animals and plants. In invertebrates, defensins represent the primary form of systemic immunity. Additionally, the complement system and phagocytic cells are utilized by most invertebrates. Ribonucleases and the RNA interference pathway are conserved across all eukaryotes and are thought to play a role in the immune response to viruses. Unlike animals, plants lack phagocytic cells, and their immune responses often involve systemic chemical signals that travel throughout the plant. When a part of a plant becomes infected, it produces a localized hypersensitive response, where cells at the infection site undergo rapid apoptosis to prevent the spread of the disease. Systemic acquired resistance (SAR) is a defensive response in plants that renders the entire plant resistant to a specific infectious agent. RNA silencing mechanisms are particularly important in this systemic response, as they can block viral replication. The immune system also plays a critical role in identifying and eliminating tumors. Tumor cells express antigens that are not found on normal cells, making them appear foreign to the immune system. These antigens can originate from oncogenic viruses, such as human papillomavirus (HPV), which causes cervical cancer, or from the organism’s own proteins that are overexpressed in tumor cells. Some tumor antigens arise from mutated proteins involved in cell growth and survival, known as oncogenes. The primary immune response to tumors involves the destruction of abnormal cells by cytotoxic T cells, often with the assistance of helper T cells. Tumor antigens are presented on major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I molecules, allowing cytotoxic T cells to recognize and target the tumor cells. Natural killer (NK) cells also play a role, particularly when tumor cells have reduced MHC class I expression, a common feature of many tumors. In some cases, antibodies are generated against tumor cells, enabling their destruction via the complement system. However, some tumors evade the immune system and progress to cancer. Tumor cells may reduce the number of MHC class I molecules on their surface, avoiding detection by cytotoxic T cells. Additionally, tumor cells can secrete immunosuppressive cytokines, such as transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β), which suppress macrophage and lymphocyte activity. Immunological tolerance may also develop against tumor antigens, preventing the immune system from attacking the tumor cells. Paradoxically, macrophages can promote tumor growth when attracted by tumor-derived cytokines, as they produce growth factors and cytokines that support tumor development. Hypoxia within the tumor microenvironment, combined with macrophage-derived cytokines, can further promote metastasis by reducing the production of proteins that inhibit cancer spread. Hormones can act as immunomodulators, influencing the sensitivity of the immune system. For instance, female sex hormones are known to stimulate both adaptive and innate immune responses, which may explain why autoimmune diseases like lupus erythematosus are more common in women and often coincide with puberty. In contrast, male sex hormones, such as testosterone, appear to suppress immune activity. Other hormones, including prolactin, growth hormone, and vitamin D, also regulate immune function. A decline in hormone levels with age is thought to contribute to weakened immune responses in older individuals. Conversely, the immune system can regulate certain hormones, such as thyroid hormone activity. The immune system is enhanced by adequate sleep and rest but impaired by stress. Diet also plays a role; fresh fruits, vegetables, and foods rich in specific fatty acids can support a healthy immune system, while fetal undernutrition can cause lifelong immune impairment. Traditional medicine suggests that certain herbs, such as echinacea, licorice, ginseng, astragalus, sage, garlic, elderberry, shiitake and lingzhi mushrooms, and hyssop, may stimulate the immune system. Studies indicate that these herbs can indeed enhance immune function, although their mechanisms of action are complex and not fully understood. In medicine, the immune response can be manipulated to suppress unwanted reactions, such as those seen in autoimmune diseases, allergies, and transplant rejection, or to stimulate protective responses against pathogens that evade the immune system. Immunosuppressive drugs are used to control autoimmune disorders, reduce inflammation, and prevent transplant rejection. Anti-inflammatory drugs are often employed to manage the effects of inflammation, but their use must be carefully controlled due to potential side effects. Lower doses of anti-inflammatory drugs are frequently combined with cytotoxic or immunosuppressive drugs, such as methotrexate or azathioprine, to achieve therapeutic effects. Cytotoxic drugs suppress the immune response by killing dividing cells, including activated T cells.
